sections.html:
Micranthemum tweediei "Monte carlo" is a popular carpet plant in the aquarium hobby. Its bright green leaves and tight creeping growth make it one of the most popular carpeting plants. It is tough and adapts to a wide range of conditions, but does best in CO2 injected tanks. Regular fertilisation and stable parameters are important for long-term health.

  • pH 5.0-8.5; tolerant of hard water.
  • Light: 50-60 µmol of PAR in CO2 injected tanks; 100+ µmol of PAR in tanks without CO2.
  • With CO2 and higher light (100 µmol of PAR), it spreads quickly; the example carpet took around 2 months to fill in fully.

Planting

Monte carlo is best planted in small bunches or single strands. Large bunches tend to float once the plant starts pearling. The plant needs to root properly to form a nice carpet, which is closely tied to good planting technique. Strands must be planted firmly in the substrate so the plant grows flat rather than upwards. Smaller clumps and individual strands give a more even carpet that roots well. Clumps that are too large dislodge easily and float. It can also be glued onto hardscape, where its roots will attach after some time.

Having adequate light (at least 50-60 µmol of PAR) and adequate CO2 also encourages creeping growth.

Solving algae issues

Freshly planted plants usually go through an adaptation phase, producing new leaves adapted to the new tank that are healthy and algae free. Plants often stop defending older leaves, and this older growth attracts algae. The solution is to remove as much old growth as possible and let the new algae-free growth spread. Old growth can never heal fully to be as robust and algae resistant as new growth.

Remove old growth by cutting and picking off older portions of the carpet, especially those badly affected by algae, using scissors and tweezers. This takes effort and time to get a well grown-in carpet.

Monte carlo is an aggressive grower, so old algae-infected portions will be covered by new growth if not removed. However, this may cause algae problems later, as older growth continues to deteriorate under the new leaves, which can stress the new top growth and attract algae.

Key success factors

  • While Monte carlo can grow in some tanks without CO2, success rates are not high. They are very high once CO2 injection is used.
  • 50-60 µmol of PAR in CO2 injected tanks; 100+ µmol of PAR in tanks without CO2 give higher success rates.
  • Good planting technique makes a huge impact on getting an even carpet. Plant in clumps as small as you can handle.
  • A stable, biologically matured tank sustains older growth in good form and prevents algae.

Trimming and propagation

It takes a while for the plant to get established. Avoid adding animals that disturb the substrate when first planting Monte carlo. Once rooted and established, it spreads at good speed. Individual strands can be cut and replanted elsewhere.

Monte carlo grows into dense mats over time. Because it is tough, such mats can keep growing on top of themselves for a long time without deteriorating. Eventually the bottoms deteriorate and the mat may detach from the substrate. Aquarists have two choices: trim regularly to keep the carpet thin, or leave it to thicken and do a large replanting when the carpet no longer grows healthy top growth because it is too thick. For Monte carlo, the second option is reasonable, as it can grow a very long time without much trimming. It may save time to do one big replanting after many months rather than smaller trimmings every couple of weeks.
